title: Comparing classical and quantum QUBO solvers: optimality, trajectory diagnostics, and limits of solver selection

paper.title:
Comparing classical
and quantum QUBO solvers: optimality, trajectory diagnostics, and limits
of solver selection
paper.abstract:
Abstract Comparing solvers for quadratic unconstrained binary optimization
(QUBO) requires distinguishing solution quality from optimality
certification. We compare classical, tensor-network, and fixed-schedule
quantum approaches on 180 benchmark instances from ten families with 14–48
variables, supplemented by harder synthetic instances with known optimal
solutions, extending to 128 variables. On the main benchmark, a general-purpose
branch-and-cut solver matches all reference energies and certifies 176
instances within a 600 s cap. When the known optima are moved to randomly
chosen bitstrings, the search comparison changes: at n = 48 n=48 the
branch-and-cut solver finds only four of ten optima and
certifies none, whereas parallel tempering reaches every optimum in every
tested run at a 60 s budget. Structural and trajectory diagnostics
explain aspects of tensor-network performance. A treewidth bound ranks
trajectory bond-dimension demand at Spearman ρ = 0.78 \rho=0.78 in sample and 0.73 0.73 out of sample, but provides only a coarse runtime estimate. Controlled
experiments identify excited-state trapping during warm-started
density-matrix renormalization group (DMRG) sweeps and demonstrate mitigation by restarting the variational search.
These diagnostics do not yield a validated solver-selection rule.
The tested linear-ramp quantum approximate optimization algorithm (LR-QAOA) runs offer no solution-quality improvement
over the classical comparators. In the separate Wishart scaling study, on
the harder setting, none of
the classical methods tested reaches the optimum at the sampled sizes
from n = 72 n=72 onward within the tested budgets.
While this does not provide evidence for quantum advantage, it identifies a domain
for further investigation.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) provides a common formulation for comparing classical, tensor-network, and quantum approaches to combinatorial optimisation Kochenberger et al. (2014) ; Lucas (2014) . For a practitioner, choosing a method requires specifying the desired outcome: a low-energy solution, an optimum, or a certificate that no better solution exists. These objectives need not favour the same solver. A meaningful comparison must therefore distinguish solution quality from optimality certification and relate both to the computational budget. These considerations connect to algorithm selection Bischl et al. (2016) , which has been investigated for classical QUBO portfolios Dunning et al. (2018) . Here, we focus on comparing solution quality, optimality certification, and computational cost across solver approaches, and on understanding how instance structure and trajectory diagnostics relate to their performance. Problem instance structure offers a possible basis for making this choice. Properties of the interaction graph can constrain the cost of exact methods and may indicate the resources required by tensor-network algorithms Markov and Shi (2008) ; Schollwöck (2011) . Quantum-information diagnostics offer a complementary perspective, but their interpretation requires care. Alongside entanglement, we measure non-stabilizerness, often called magic : a quantum resource that characterises departures from stabilizer states, which admit efficient classical simulation Gottesman (1998) ; Aaronson and Gottesman (2004) ; Leone et al. (2022) . Magic concerns the resources needed for stabilizer-based simulation but high magic alone (e.g., with low entanglement) does not rule out efficient classical simulation by methods that do not rely on a stabilizer representation. Every QUBO optimum can be represented by a computational-basis state with neither entanglement nor magic. The relevant resources consequently arise in the intermediate states explored by an algorithm, rather than in the optimal bitstring itself Dupont et al. (2022b) ; Dupont et al. (2022a) ; Capecci et al. (2025) . We study these resources along a transverse-field interpolation connecting a simple initial Hamiltonian to the QUBO Hamiltonian Kadowaki and Nishimori (1998) ; Albash and Lidar (2018) . This paper investigates how much structural and trajectory information can explain solver performance, and whether it supports useful choices between methods. We compare a general-purpose branch-and-cut solver (Gurobi) Gurobi Optimization, LLC (2024) , simulated annealing (SA) Kirkpatrick et al. (1983) , a density-matrix renormalization group (DMRG) based tensor-network (TN) anneal White (1992) ; Schollwöck (2011) , and fixed-schedule linear-ramp quantum approximate optimization (LR-QAOA) Farhi et al. (2014) ; Montañez-Barrera and Michielsen (2025) , with parallel tempering (PT) Swendsen and Wang (1986) ; Hukushima and Nemoto (1996) providing an additional classical comparison. Each serves a specific role: branch-and-cut supplies a baseline capable of certification, SA supplies a simple thermal-search baseline and PT tests whether SA’s failures persist under a stronger thermal method. The DMRG anneal probes variational optimisation of matrix-product states (MPS), while LR-QAOA probes a quantum-circuit approach with prescribed parameters. The shared Hamiltonian interpolation connects these last two methods, although their computational procedures and intermediate states remain distinct. Our main benchmark (Campaign A) comprises 180 instances from ten problem families with n = 14 n=14 – 48 48 variables. It includes 90 small calibration instances with exhaustively verified optima and 90 larger instances used to assess extrapolation; the latter also receive an exact-solver cross-check (Sec. 2.3 ). The robustness controls (Campaign B) and scaling study (Campaign E) also use the Wishart-planted family Hamze et al. (2020) : synthetic problems constructed from random Gaussian vectors so that a chosen solution is guaranteed to be optimal, with a parameter controlling problem difficulty. These known optima provide reference targets beyond the range of exhaustive enumeration. To avoid giving solvers an easily guessed target, we randomly complement selected binary variables ( x i ↦ 1 − x i x_{i}\mapsto 1-x_{i} ) and transform the objective accordingly. This relabelling, called gauge randomisation , moves the planted optimum from the all-zero bitstring to a random bitstring while preserving the energy landscape. It controls for the advantage a solver may gain from the original placement of the solution Mandrà and Katzgraber (2018) . These experiments examine the robustness of the comparison and extend the study to n = 128 n=128 (Secs. 3.3 and 6 ). The results distinguish three aspects of solver performance. First, branch-and-cut provides a strong baseline in Campaign A, matching every reference energy and certifying nearly all instances. Its advantage nevertheless depends on whether the task is search or certification: on the harder gauge-randomised instances, PT can find optima that branch-and-cut misses within its allotted budget (Secs. 3.3 and 6 ). Second, a cheap treewidth bound of the QUBO interaction graph ranks the bond-dimension demand of the tensor-network trajectories, but supplies only a coarse runtime estimate. The evaluated structural features and cost models do not produce a useful solver-selection rule (Sec. 4.3 ). Controlled experiments further identify excited-state trapping during warm-started DMRG sweeps as a failure mechanism that can be mitigated by restarting the variational search (Sec. 4 ). Entanglement and magic are only moderately correlated in the measured trajectories and provide distinct diagnostic information. Third, the tested LR-QAOA runs provide no solution-quality improvement over the classical comparators (Sec. 5 ). The larger Wishart experiments identify instances on which the tested classical methods struggle, offering a concrete setting for further quantum–classical comparisons. Together, these findings establish a classical baseline, clarify what trajectory diagnostics can explain, and identify the additional evidence needed for meaningful solver selection across computational approaches. Section 2 defines the shared framework and summarises Campaigns A–E. Section 3 presents the main benchmark and robustness controls (A and B). Section 4 brings together the benchmark diagnostics and targeted TN mechanism tests (C). Section 5 reports the LR-QAOA comparison and supplementary quantum studies (D), followed by the Wishart scaling study (E) in Sec. 6 . Supporting experiments and exploratory resource projections are collected in App. 11 .

sections.heading: 2 Problem formulation and experimental framework
sections.text: This section defines the optimisation problem, the benchmark instances, and the common evaluation framework. We distinguish solution quality, optimality certification, and computational cost. The main benchmark provides the basis for the solver comparison and predictive analyses; additional campaigns examine robustness, tensor-network failure mechanisms, LR-QAOA protocols, and scaling to harder instances. Section 2.6 summarises their questions and coverage.

sections.heading: 2.1 QUBO formulation and Hamiltonian interpolation
sections.text: We consider QUBO instances defined by a real symmetric matrix Q ∈ ℝ n × n Q\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n} , with the objective E ∗ = min x ∈ { 0 , 1 } n ⁡ x T ​ Q ​ x . E^{*}=\min_{x\in\{0,1\}^{n}}x^{T}Qx. Introducing classical spin variables z i ∈ { − 1 , 1 } z_{i}\in\{-1,1\} through x i = ( 1 − z i ) / 2 x_{i}=(1-z_{i})/2 gives the Ising form E ⁡ ( z ) = ∑ i < j J i ​ j ​ z i ​ z j + ∑ i h i ​ z i + c , E(z)=\sum_{i<j}J_{ij}z_{i}z_{j}+\sum_{i}h_{i}z_{i}+c, (1) where J i ​ j = Q i ​ j / 2 J_{ij}=Q_{ij}/2 , h i = − Q i ​ i / 2 − 1 2 ∑ j ≠ i Q i ​ j h_{i}=-Q_{ii}/2-\tfrac{1}{2}\sum_{j\neq i}Q_{ij} , and c = 1 2 ​ ∑ i Q i ​ i + 1 2 ​ ∑ i < j Q i ​ j c=\tfrac{1}{2}\sum_{i}Q_{ii}+\tfrac{1}{2}\sum_{i<j}Q_{ij} for this symmetric-matrix convention Lucas (2014) . The additive constant preserves the objective value but does not affect which bitstrings minimise it. Replacing each spin variable by the Pauli- Z i Z_{i} operator gives the diagonal cost Hamiltonian H Z = ∑ i < j J i ​ j ​ Z i ​ Z j + ∑ i h i ​ Z i + c ​ I , H_{Z}=\sum_{i<j}J_{ij}Z_{i}Z_{j}+\sum_{i}h_{i}Z_{i}+cI, where I I is the identity operator. We retain the constant here so that the eigenvalue associated with | x ⟩ \lvert x\rangle equals x T ​ Q ​ x x^{T}Qx . Every optimal bitstring defines a computational-basis ground state of H Z H_{Z} , with zero entanglement and zero magic. A degenerate ground space may also contain superpositions with nonzero quantum resources. Thus the resources of an optimal bitstring alone do not distinguish instance difficulty; we instead examine the intermediate states produced by specified computational procedures Dupont et al. (2022b) ; Dupont et al. (2022a) ; Capecci et al. (2025) . The Hamiltonian interpolation used in this study is H ( s ) = − ( 1 − s ) ∑ i X i + s H Z , s ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] , H(s)=-(1-s)\sum_{i}X_{i}+s\,H_{Z},\qquad s\in[0,1], (2) where X i X_{i} is the Pauli- X X operator on spin i i . At s = 0 s=0 , the ground state is the product state | + ⟩ ⊗ n \lvert+\rangle^{\otimes n} , with | + ⟩ = ( | 0 ⟩ + | 1 ⟩ ) / 2 \lvert+\rangle=(\lvert 0\rangle+\lvert 1\rangle)/\sqrt{2} ; at s = 1 s=1 , the Hamiltonian is H Z H_{Z} . This interpolation provides a common Hamiltonian framework for the methods considered here. Quantum annealing evolves under a time-dependent Hamiltonian along this path. LR-QAOA uses alternating mixer and cost unitaries related to a discretisation of that evolution, with the coefficient normalisation and schedule specified in App. 10 . The DMRG anneal instead performs successive variational optimisations at selected values of s s . These procedures need not produce the same intermediate states. In particular, the entanglement measured along a DMRG sweep does not by itself bound the entanglement of the corresponding LR-QAOA circuit. The interpolation thus connects the computational approaches without identifying their intermediate states. We next specify the instances on which they are compared and the reference energies used to evaluate their outputs.

sections.heading: 2.2.1 Calibration and out-of-sample evaluation
sections.text: The main benchmark comprises 180 benchmark instances, indexed by problem family, requested size, and instance-generation seed. This count follows the benchmark’s family–size–seed combinations; it does not imply 180 distinct problem matrices. We use distinct instances when matrix uniqueness matters and runs for solver executions. The benchmark is split into two sets by instance size: • The calibration set contains 90 instances at requested sizes n req ∈ { 14 , 18 , 22 } n_{\mathrm{req}}\in\{14,18,22\} . The grid family has actual sizes n ∈ { 15 , 20 , 24 } n\in\{15,20,24\} ; all other families retain the requested sizes, giving an overall range n = 14 n=14 – 24 24 . All reference optima are verified by exhaustive enumeration. This set is used to fit the runtime models in App. 12 . • The out-of-sample set contains 90 instances at requested sizes n req ∈ { 32 , 40 , 48 } n_{\mathrm{req}}\in\{32,40,48\} . The grid family has actual sizes n ∈ { 35 , 42 , 48 } n\in\{35,42,48\} ; all other families retain the requested sizes. Their reference energies are known by construction or analytically, or certified by the exact-solver cross-check, except for one SK instance whose reference remains best-known (Sec. 2.3 ). For a requested size n req n_{\mathrm{req}} , the grid generator uses a = ⌊ n req ⌋ a=\lfloor\sqrt{n_{\mathrm{req}}}\rfloor rows and b = ⌈ n req / a ⌉ b=\lceil n_{\mathrm{req}}/a\rceil columns, giving n = a ​ b n=ab variables. This is a generator convention, not a restriction on permissible grids. The 3-regular generator increases odd requested sizes by one, but all requested sizes in this benchmark are even. The grid and ferromagnetic-chain families have no random parameters, so their generators do not depend on the seed. For these families, the three benchmark instances at each size share the same matrix. Solving them therefore repeats the computation on that matrix rather than sampling three independently generated problems. Each split thus contains 78 distinct matrices, 156 in total. Rank correlations between instance features are reported over the distinct matrices, since the repeated matrices would otherwise enter them three times. This split tests for size extrapolation rather than interpolation within a randomly partitioned size range. The reported out-of-sample runtime errors use models fitted on the calibration set. Exploratory analyses using all instances, including success-probability weighting, are identified separately in App. 12 .

sections.heading: 2.2.2 Wishart extensions and optimum placement
sections.text: The additional Wishart studies use known planted optima to evaluate search beyond the range of exhaustive enumeration. The aspect ratio α = M / n \alpha=M/n controls the ensemble, with the main benchmark using M = ⌊ 0.7 ​ n ⌋ M=\lfloor 0.7n\rfloor and the scaling study also considering α = 0.5 \alpha=0.5 (Sec. 6 ). The original construction of these instances places an optimum at the all-zero bitstring. To test sensitivity to this special placement, we use gauge-transformed variants: selected binary variables are complemented and the objective and reference energy are transformed accordingly. This moves the planted optimum to a generic bitstring while preserving the landscape up to relabelling and an accounted-for additive energy shift. Original and gauged variants form a paired comparison, not independent instance samples. The control subsets and repetitions are specified in Sec. 3.3 ; the larger scaling study has its own instance set and budgets.

sections.heading: 2.3 Reference energies and optimality status
sections.text: We denote E ∗ = min x ∈ { 0 , 1 } n ⁡ x T ​ Q ​ x E^{*}=\min_{x\in\{0,1\}^{n}}x^{T}Qx as the true global minimum and additionally denote the benchmark target by E ref E_{\mathrm{ref}} . This reference energy is the objective value against which a solver’s returned solution is scored. When it is established by exhaustive enumeration, solver certification, an analytic argument, or a planted construction, E ref = E ∗ E_{\mathrm{ref}}=E^{*} . Otherwise it is the best-known feasible value, so E ref ≥ E ∗ E_{\mathrm{ref}}\geq E^{*} . A hit of a solver means matching E ref E_{\mathrm{ref}} within the tolerance defined in Sec. 2.5.4 ; it implies reaching the optimum only when the reference is known to be optimal. Solver-certified references use the numerical optimality convention specified in Sec. 2.4 . The reference construction and its optimality status depend on size and family. For all instance families at n ≤ 24 n\leq 24 , exhaustive enumeration returns the exact optimum with a proof. All 90 calibration instances are of this kind. For Wishart, grid, exact cover, and ferro-chain instances at all sizes, the optimum is planted or known analytically, independently of any solver: the Wishart ensemble is generated around a chosen ground-state configuration Hamze et al. (2020) ; a bipartite grid Max-Cut has E ∗ = − m E^{*}=-m , where m m is the number of edges (every edge can be cut); the exact-cover instances are built around a hidden exact partition; and the ferromagnetic chain is minimised by the aligned configuration. These constructions provide E ref = E ∗ E_{\mathrm{ref}}=E^{*} for 36 of the 90 out-of-sample instances, without requiring exhaustive enumeration. Of the remaining 54 out-of-sample instances (dense and sparse ER, 3-regular, MIS, random frustrated, and SK), 53 have reference energies certified as optimal by branch-and-cut. The sole exception is one SK instance at n = 48 n=48 . For this instance, E ref E_{\mathrm{ref}} is the best-known feasible energy, reached by both an extended SA run and branch-and-cut, but not certified within the exact solver’s time limit. The extended SA budget is specified in Sec. 2.4 . Thus E ref = E ∗ E_{\mathrm{ref}}=E^{*} is established for 179 of the 180 main benchmark instances: 90 by enumeration, 36 larger instances by construction or analytic arguments, and the remaining 53 by the exact-solver check. Equality remains unverified only for the SK instance identified above. In the additional Wishart experiments, including the larger scaling study, the references remain known optima by construction, independently of solver success.

sections.heading: 2.4 Solver approaches and main-benchmark configurations
sections.text: We compare an exact optimisation baseline with thermal-search and tensor-network heuristics, and a quantum-circuit heuristic. Table 2 summarises their computational budgets. The descriptions below explain the choices needed to interpret the comparison; numerical settings and implementation checks are collected in App. 10 .

sections.heading: Exact solver.
sections.text: Branch-and-cut searches restricted subproblems and uses bounds, strengthened by additional constraints, to discard regions that cannot improve the best solution found and ultimately certify optimality. We use Gurobi Kochenberger et al. (2014) ; Gurobi Optimization, LLC (2024) , which minimises the binary quadratic objective, using either a linearised or a native quadratic formulation, with a 600 600 s time limit. Finding the reference energy and certifying optimality are distinct outcomes: the reported certificate flag denotes the solver’s optimal status under its numerical tolerances (Sec. 2.3 ). Exhaustive enumeration provides an independent cross-check at small sizes. This general-purpose baseline does not establish the limits of exact optimisation: specialised branch-and-cut Rehfeldt et al. (2023) or methods exploiting low treewidth may perform better.

sections.heading: Simulated annealing.
sections.text: SA Kirkpatrick et al. (1983) explores bitstrings through single-variable flips, accepting some energy increases to escape local minima. Metropolis acceptance becomes less permissive as the temperature falls. We use a geometric cooling schedule. Each run comprises four restarts of 2000 sweeps, where a sweep proposes one update per variable. The best state from each restart is refined by single-flip local search, and the lowest energy is returned. The extended runs used to establish reference energies receive four times this update budget.

sections.heading: Parallel tempering.
sections.text: Similar to SA, PT Swendsen and Wang (1986) ; Hukushima and Nemoto (1996) runs several searches at different temperatures and exchanges configurations between them, allowing low-temperature searches to benefit from exploration at higher temperatures. As a second thermal-search baseline, we use 16 replicas with exchange attempts after every sweep. It uses a wall-clock budget and receives no final local-search polish. It is reported alongside SA but is not included in the retrospective heuristic winner labels or assigned a fitted runtime model. The main and control budgets are summarised in Table 2 and Sec. 3.3 .

sections.heading: Tensor-network anneal.
sections.text: The TN anneal approximately minimises the interpolating Hamiltonian within a compact MPS representation, using each state as the starting point for the next interpolation step. We use two-site DMRG White (1992) ; Schollwöck (2011) , with bond dimension capped at χ = 32 \chi=32 . The bond dimension controls the size of the MPS representation and limits the entanglement it can represent. Cold-start checks mitigate excited-state trapping (Sec. 4 ). Several candidate bitstrings are extracted from the final MPS, each is refined by single-flip local search, and the lowest energy is returned. Separate runs at χ = 4 , 8 , 16 \chi=4,8,16 assess sensitivity to the bond cap. These optimisation runs all enable reset checks. The trajectory diagnostics use separate, reset-free sweeps (Sec. 2.5.2 ).

sections.heading: LR-QAOA.
sections.text: LR-QAOA prepares a quantum state by alternating operations determined by the objective with operations that mix computational-basis states, then samples bitstrings as candidate solutions. It uses fixed linear parameter schedules on a coefficient-normalised Hamiltonian Montañez-Barrera and Michielsen (2025) . Here, a quantum circuit is the sequence of quantum gates that prepares the state before sampling. All LR-QAOA results reported in this paper are obtained by classical simulation of such circuits, none are quantum-hardware executions. The number of LR-QAOA layers is denoted by p p , and Δ \Delta sets the amplitude of the linear parameter schedules. With m m nonzero pairwise couplings, the LR-QAOA circuit uses p ​ m pm logical two-qubit cost gates. The layer count p p differs from the gate-level circuit depth D D , which also accounts for how gates within a layer are scheduled (App. 11.3 ). Campaign A uses exact statevector simulation for n ≤ 16 n\leq 16 and approximate MPS simulation for 16 < n ≤ 32 16<n\leq 32 , subject to a limit of 3000 logical two-qubit cost gates. Table 2 gives the depths and sampling budgets. Runs replaced by SA because of these limits are excluded from quantum comparisons. The lowest-energy sampled bitstring is selected and then polished once by single-flip local search. Unlike TN, this does not polish every candidate. The separate depth-scaling and adaptive-depth studies are discussed in Sec. 5 . Agreement between the statevector and MPS simulators at small size checks implementation conventions, but does not establish convergence of the larger MPS simulations. Nor do the DMRG trajectory diagnostics bound entanglement in the LR-QAOA states (Sec. 2.1 ). The MPS results must therefore be interpreted as approximate simulations of LR-QAOA.

sections.text: These features use the instance data and a small local-search probe, without a quantum-state simulation. The interaction graph G = ( V , E G ) G=(V,E_{G}) has one vertex per binary variable and an edge ( i , j ) (i,j) wherever J i ​ j ≠ 0 J_{ij}\neq 0 . Its edge count is m = | E G | m=|E_{G}| . Treewidth bound tw ^ \widehat{\mathrm{tw}} . The treewidth of the interaction graph measures how far the graph is from a tree: a tree decomposition of width w w groups the vertices into overlapping “bags” of size w + 1 w+1 arranged in a tree, such that every edge lies inside some bag and the bags containing any given vertex form a connected subtree. Its operational meaning here is that both exact dynamic programming over such a decomposition and exact tensor-network contraction cost exp ⁡ [ O ⁡ ( tw ) ] \exp[O(\mathrm{tw})] Markov and Shi (2008) ; Dumitrescu et al. (2018) : the treewidth is the size of the “interface” a contraction must carry along, and hence directly the exponent of the tensor-network cost. Computing tw \mathrm{tw} exactly is NP-hard, so we use the standard min-degree/min-fill elimination heuristics and take the smaller bound, tw ^ ≥ tw \widehat{\mathrm{tw}}\geq\mathrm{tw} . The two are kept apart throughout: tw \mathrm{tw} is the exact treewidth, in which all cost statements and the structural descriptions of the instance families are phrased, while tw ^ \widehat{\mathrm{tw}} is the computed bound, the quantity the pipeline actually reads. A chain has tw = 1 \mathrm{tw}=1 and a fully connected graph on n n vertices has tw = n − 1 \mathrm{tw}=n-1 . Two distinct tensor-network computations appear in this paper and should not be conflated. The first is the exact contraction just described, equivalently dynamic programming over a tree decomposition, which returns the optimum together with a proof of optimality at a cost exp ⁡ [ O ⁡ ( tw ) ] \exp[O(\mathrm{tw})] . It is what gives tw ^ \widehat{\mathrm{tw}} its operational meaning, and it is the method behind the bounded-treewidth rule R3 of App. 12 : once tw ^ \widehat{\mathrm{tw}} is small enough for this contraction to be affordable, the instance can be settled exactly and no heuristic cost has to be estimated. The second is our solver (Sec. 2.4 ): a variational matrix-product-state anneal, a heuristic with no optimality guarantee, whose cost is polynomial in a bond dimension χ \chi that is not fixed by tw \mathrm{tw} a priori. That larger tw ^ \widehat{\mathrm{tw}} nevertheless means larger realised χ \chi is a measured result of this work (Sec. 4 ), not a definition, and it is what licenses putting tw ^ \widehat{\mathrm{tw}} into the solver’s runtime model, Eq. ( 12 ). The coupling dynamic range D J D_{J} is the ratio of the strongest to the weakest coupling, using J i ​ j J_{ij} from Eq. ( 1 ): D J = max ( i , j ) ∈ E G ⁡ | J i ​ j | min ( i , j ) ∈ E G ⁡ | J i ​ j | , D_{J}\;=\;\frac{\max_{(i,j)\in E_{G}}|J_{ij}|}{\min_{(i,j)\in E_{G}}|J_{ij}|}, (3) A large ratio indicates separated coupling scales, which can make single-spin thermal exploration difficult: temperatures that resolve weak couplings may suppress rearrangements involving strong couplings. In Campaign A this does not separate SA successes from failures (Sec. 3.1 ). The Wishart scaling study instead varies the construction parameter α = M / n \alpha=M/n (Sec. 6 ). The implementation includes only couplings with | J i ​ j | > 10 − 15 |J_{ij}|>10^{-15} and sets the ratio to one if none remain. Four cheap graph quantities and one landscape probe complete Tier 0. Density is ρ G = 2 ​ m / [ n ⁡ ( n − 1 ) ] \rho_{G}=2m/[n(n-1)] . The graph bandwidth b RCM b_{\mathrm{RCM}} is taken after a reverse Cuthill–McKee reordering Cuthill and McKee (1969) , which clusters the adjacency matrix’s nonzeros around the diagonal. The resulting bandwidth measures how far the interaction graph is from a one-dimensional chain, and hence how well a matrix-product state, intrinsically 1-D once a site ordering is fixed, can cover the couplings. Frustration enters twice, as exact signed-graph balance Harary (1953) and as the sampled fraction of frustrated triangles f △ f_{\triangle} Toulouse (1977) . A cycle is frustrated when no spin assignment satisfies all its bonds. Planarity is tested because it admits a polynomial exact algorithm for field-free Max-Cut Hadlock (1975) . The landscape probe is the multi-start local-minimum hit rate h LM h_{\mathrm{LM}} : 50 descents from random bitstrings use seeds seed + 1000 ​ r \mathrm{seed}+1000r , r = 0 , … , 49 r=0,\ldots,49 . The rate is the fraction reaching the best energy among these 50 descents, using the same mixed tolerance as the hit criterion in Eq. ( 5 ). The triangle probe checks all triangles if there are at most 20,000, or randomly samples 20,000 without replacement. A frustrated cycle has negative product of sign ⁡ ( − J i ​ j ) \operatorname{sign}(-J_{ij}) ; graph balance tests the corresponding bond constraints.

sections.heading: 2.5.2 Trajectory diagnostics (Tier 1; n ≲ 10 2 n\lesssim 10^{2} )
sections.text: At each interpolation point in Eq. ( 2 ), two-site DMRG White (1992) ; Schollwöck (2011) seeks a low-energy MPS approximation, initialised from the preceding point. The resulting sequence defines the diagnostic trajectory. It is not guaranteed to follow the instantaneous ground state: warm starting can retain an excited branch, as investigated in Sec. 4 . The measured resources refer to these variational states, with their specified site ordering and bond-dimension caps. The entanglement probe uses χ = 16 \chi=16 and the magic probe uses χ = 4 \chi=4 , in separate DMRG sweeps on the nine-point uniform grid s ∈ { 0 , 0.125 , 0.25 , … , 1 } s\in\{0,0.125,0.25,\ldots,1\} . Neither probe enables the branch-reset mechanism used by the optimisation solver. Magic is computed on the states retained from the χ = 4 \chi=4 sweep, while S vN max S_{\mathrm{vN}}^{\max} and χ 99 max \chi_{99}^{\max} come from the dedicated χ = 16 \chi=16 sweep. The diagnostic and solver trajectories thus differ in grid and reset configuration. The entanglement barrier is measured by cutting the chain at bond b b and Schmidt decomposing, which gives probabilities p 1 ≥ p 2 ≥ … p_{1}\geq p_{2}\geq\dots . The von Neumann entropy S vN ( b ; s ) = − ∑ a p a log 2 p a S_{\mathrm{vN}}(b;s)=-\sum_{a}p_{a}\log_{2}p_{a} measures how much quantum correlation crosses that cut, and χ 99 ​ ( b , s ) = min ⁡ { k : ∑ a ≤ k p a ≥ 0.99 } \chi_{99}(b;s)=\min\{k:\sum_{a\leq k}p_{a}\geq 0.99\} is the number of Schmidt components needed to retain 99 % 99\% of the weight across that cut of the computed state. We record maxima over the sampled interpolation points and all cuts, S vN max S_{\mathrm{vN}}^{\max} and χ 99 max \chi_{99}^{\max} . The largest recorded χ 99 max \chi_{99}^{\max} is 13 in each split. Being below the bond-dimension cap does not alone establish convergence. The reset-enabled χ = 32 \chi=32 solver trajectories (Sec. 2.4 ) record values up to 20 and exceed the diagnostic value on 64 of 90 calibration and 77 of 90 out-of-sample instances; the two agree in rank at Spearman ρ = 0.69 \rho=0.69 and 0.73 0.73 . The diagnostic χ 99 max \chi_{99}^{\max} is therefore a ranking proxy for the representation demand of the solver’s trajectory, not a measurement of it. For comparison, a Haar-random n n -qubit pure state has half-cut entropy approximately n / 2 n/2 bits Page (1993) , with bond-dimension requirements growing exponentially in n n . The measured trajectories can be compared with this reference scale without assuming that low entanglement ensures successful optimisation. Entanglement alone does not decide classical simulability. Stabilizer states, those preparable by Clifford circuits, can be maximally entangled yet are simulable in polynomial time by the Gottesman–Knill theorem Gottesman (1998) ; Aaronson and Gottesman (2004) . What obstructs such stabilizer-based simulation is non-stabilizerness , or “magic”: the departure of a state from the stabilizer class. We quantify it with the stabilizer 2-Rényi entropy Leone et al. (2022) M 2 ( | ψ ⟩ ) = − log 2 ( 2 − n ∑ P ⟨ ψ | P | ψ ⟩ 4 ) , M_{2}(\lvert\psi\rangle)=-\log_{2}\Bigl(2^{-n}\sum_{P}\langle\psi\rvert P\lvert\psi\rangle^{4}\Bigr), (4) the sum running over all 4 n 4^{n} Pauli strings. M 2 = 0 M_{2}=0 exactly for stabilizer states (their Pauli spectrum is flat on the stabilizer group) and grows with magic. It is computable exactly on an MPS by a four-replica transfer contraction Haug and Piroli (2023) , which is what makes it usable here. The contraction is exact for the supplied MPS but the state itself is an approximation. At the χ = 4 \chi=4 probe cap, M 2 max M_{2}^{\max} is therefore a truncated estimate. It is used in rank correlations and in the 8-bit threshold of Eq. ( 8 ), not as a converged value for the exact state. That threshold has no independent motivation: it was set on the Campaign A data themselves (App. 11.3 ). The initial state | + ⟩ ⊗ n \lvert+\rangle^{\otimes n} has zero magic. A final computational-basis state also has zero magic, but this need not hold for every superposition in a degenerate ground space. Figure 1 illustrates the measured profiles on one instance. Magic and entanglement probe different aspects of state representation. Neither a small measured magic value nor a large one, on its own, establishes the cost of all classical simulation methods. sections.text: For small instances ( n ≲ 20 n\lesssim 20 ), sparse diagonalisation of H ⁡ ( s ) H(s) provides an independent comparison with the DMRG energies and resolves the levels used in the trapping analysis (Fig. 5 ). This check applies only at the sizes where the spectrum is computed. The campaign-specific grids and eigensolver settings are given in App. 11.1 . Let E 0 ​ ( s ) ≤ E 1 ​ ( s ) ≤ ⋯ E_{0}(s)\leq E_{1}(s)\leq\cdots be the ordered eigenvalues, and let g g denote the ground-state degeneracy of the final cost Hamiltonian H Z H_{Z} . At s = 1 s=1 , the first g g levels share the optimal energy, so E 1 − E 0 E_{1}-E_{0} vanishes whenever g > 1 g>1 , independently of solver difficulty. We record Δ g ​ ( s ) = E g ​ ( s ) − E 0 ​ ( s ) \Delta_{g}(s)=E_{g}(s)-E_{0}(s) to avoid this endpoint degeneracy in the reported diagnostic. At s = 1 s=1 it is the gap above the optimal manifold. At intermediate s s , the first g g levels need not be degenerate, so this definition should not be identified automatically with the instantaneous ground-state excitation gap. The n ≲ 20 n\lesssim 20 ceiling is the 2 n 2^{n} wall: the calculation lives in the full Hilbert space ( 10 6 10^{6} dimensions at n = 20 n=20 ), is repeated at every point of the s s -grid, and must resolve the entire g g -fold manifold plus one level above it, so degeneracy multiplies the eigenvalue count. Omitting it above n = 20 n=20 costs nothing operationally: no Tier-0 feature, no cost model of Eqs. ( 10 )–( 12 ), and no term of the quantum indicator Eq. sections.text: The experiments are organised into five campaigns, summarised in Table 4 . Each campaign addresses a specific question through a defined choice of problem instances, solver configurations, and repetitions. sections.heading: 3.2 Sensitivity to stochastic repetition (Campaign B)
sections.text: Because SA is stochastic, a single run may not reliably characterise its performance on an instance. To assess this variability and estimate reference-hit rates, we repeat SA at the main budget using ten seeds on each of the 180 benchmark instances (1800 scored runs). Separate runs at the Campaign A seeds reproduce all 180 recorded energies. These checks are excluded from the repeat hit rates. SA reaches the optimum in all 900 benchmark runs on the calibration instances and in at least 98 % 98\% of runs on non-Wishart out-of-sample instances. For Wishart, the repetitions qualify the Campaign A single-run outcomes. For the six ungauged Campaign A Wishart instances at n = 40 , 48 n=40,48 , 32 of 60 additional SA runs reach the planted optimum ( 53.3 % 53.3\% ), compared with one of six Campaign A runs ( 16.7 % 16.7\% ). This repeat control shows that the Campaign A single-run outcomes understate SA’s success rate on these instances. It is distinct from the paired gauge comparison below. The additional PT baseline uses ten runs per benchmark instance at a fixed 0.75 0.75 s budget. Its reported aggregate hit rate is 0.982 0.982 , compared with 0.981 0.981 for the SA repetitions. A restricted TN repeatability check ran three anneals on each of the three ungauged Campaign A Wishart instances at n = 40 n=40 . The returned energies were bit-identical within each instance. This concerns only those three matrices and does not establish determinism of TN optimisation in general.

sections.heading: 3.3 Effect of planted-optimum placement (Campaign B)
sections.text: The strong Gurobi comparison in Campaign A leaves open whether the fixed placement of the planted Wishart optimum aids search and hence presents a bias. The paired control experiment hence tries to isolate that effect. Building on that, the enlarged set broadens the instance sample.

sections.heading: Paired optimum-placement control.
sections.text: For the Wishart instances, we test whether solver performance depends on the placement of the planted optimum, comparing each ungauged instance with a gauge-transformed copy. Hence, we re-solve the nine Wishart instances at n = 32 , 40 , 48 n=32,40,48 both as generated and after random spin reversals. The gauge transformation described in Sec. 2.2 is checked against exhaustive enumeration at small sizes. This paired comparison tests sensitivity to solution placement Mandrà and Katzgraber (2018) . In the paired control at n = 32 n=32 and 40 40 , branch-and-cut proves optimality in both frames. The medians of the six per-instance gauged/plain ratios are 2.2 2.2 for full solver-wrapper runtime and 1.2 1.2 for node count. At n = 48 n=48 , branch-and-cut finds the optimum on all three ungauged instances, but on only one of their gauged counterparts. This reduction suggests that the all-zero placement (ungauged) helped branch-and-cut find an optimum on these instances.

sections.heading: 4 Tensor-network diagnostics, failure mechanisms, and solver selection
sections.text: We first analyse measurements from Campaign A, then use the targeted experiments in Campaign C to investigate failure mechanisms. These analyses distinguish representation demand, runtime, and search success.

sections.heading: 4.1 Structural prediction of representation demand and runtime
sections.text: The bond-dimension demand χ 99 max \chi_{99}^{\max} along the TN trajectory correlates with the O ⁡ ( n 3 ) O(n^{3}) treewidth bound at ρ = 0.78 \rho=0.78 on the calibration set and 0.73 0.73 out of sample, and with the cheaper RCM bandwidth at ρ = 0.72 \rho=0.72 and 0.67 0.67 (Fig. 3 ). These values are computed over the 78 distinct matrices of each split (Sec. 2.2.1 ); counting the repeated grid and ferro-chain matrices three times would raise them to 0.81 0.81 and 0.76 0.76 . This is a reliable ranking, not a precise cost estimate: the regression explains 55 % 55\% of the variance in log 2 ⁡ χ 99 max \log_{2}\chi_{99}^{\max} on the distinct calibration matrices ( R 2 = 0.55 R^{2}=0.55 ). With measured χ 99 max \chi_{99}^{\max} , the runtime model predicts wall-clock to a median factor of 1.8 1.8 out of sample. Using treewidth alone, the genuinely a-priori median factor is 7.6 7.6 (Sec. 4.3 ). It therefore supports coarse cost comparisons. That predictability does not imply that TN is fast. Among the 44 44 instances whose trajectory needs only χ 99 ≤ 2 \chi_{99}\leq 2 , its anneal is a median 17 × 17\times slower than SA. At n = 48 n=48 the median gap is 1600 × 1600\times . This supports treating them as complementary, rather than interchangeable, diagnostics of the computed states.

sections.heading: 4.2 Capacity sensitivity, trapping, and reset mitigation (Campaign C)
sections.text: Modest measured representation demand does not ensure successful variational optimisation. Campaign C compares reset-enabled solver runs at χ = 4 , 8 , 16 \chi=4,8,16 and examines selected trajectories against independently computed spectra. These runs differ from the reset-free diagnostic sweeps in Sec. 2.5.2 . Detailed spectral settings and the capacity-failure breakdown are given in App. 11.1 . The targeted trajectories identify excited-state trapping as a failure mechanism. A warm-started sweep initialises each s s -point from the preceding converged state and can follow an excited spectral branch through an avoided crossing instead of the branch that becomes the ground state. On 3-regular Max-Cut, trapped runs end in excited computational-basis states at a median normalised distance d H min / n = 0.40 d_{H}^{\min}/n=0.40 from the nearest optimum, whereas successful runs end at an optimum (Fig. 5 ). We tested a crossing-detection reset: at checkpoints in the second half of the sweep, we launch a cold-started DMRG from a fresh MPS and replace the warm-started state if the new state has lower energy. This cures all previously resistant cases with one anneal: over the eight evaluated instances ( 3 3 -regular Max-Cut and ferromagnetic controls at n = 18 n=18 and 22 22 ) the reset reaches the optimum on 8 8 of 8 8 , against 5 5 of 8 8 for the baseline and 6 6 of 8 8 for four-fold multi-seeding, and the cost-optimised variant requires exactly one reset per cure. With trapping controlled, capacity failures are rare: among the 81 81 mitigation-clean out-of-sample instances, one fails at χ = 4 \chi=4 and none at χ = 16 \chi=16 . The remaining failures are not nested in bond cap, consistent with residual trapping rather than a simple capacity limit. The diagnostic χ 99 max \chi_{99}^{\max} does not meet the stated discrimination target. Detailed counts and AUC values are given in App. 11.1 . sections.heading: 4.3 Limits of predictive solver selection
sections.text: To assess whether runtime prediction supports heuristic selection, we fit cost models on the 90 calibration instances and evaluate them on the 90 larger instances from Campaign A (App. 12 ). The accuracy summarised above concerns runtime. Selecting a solver additionally requires information about its probability of reaching the target. These cost predictions do not provide a useful selection rule. The cost-based ranking matches the single-run ex-post heuristic label on 85 85 of 90 90 out-of-sample instances, but an always-predict-SA baseline scores identically and the balanced accuracy is 0.50 0.50 . The ranking never selects TN. Moreover, the five apparent misses are Wishart benchmark instances from Campaign A with single-run labels, while repeated SA and PT runs show that those isolated observations are not stable solver properties. The model predicts runtime, not the probability of reaching the target. Success-probability weighting does not resolve this limitation (App. 12 ). Runtime prediction provides limited information about cost, but does not supply the success-probability information needed for a useful heuristic selection rule on these instances.

sections.heading: 5 Quantum comparison and limits of extrapolation
sections.text: The main LR-QAOA comparison belongs to Campaign A. Campaign D tests adaptive-depth coverage, larger-instance simulation convergence, and small-size success-probability scaling on separate instance sets.

sections.heading: 5.1 Main LR-QAOA comparison and supplementary checks
sections.text: LR-QAOA produces no solution-quality win in the 105 simulation runs: it never beats the better of SA and the TN anneal. These comprise 30 exact statevector runs at n ≤ 16 n\leq 16 and 75 MPS-proxy runs at 18 ≤ n ≤ 32 18\leq n\leq 32 . It underperforms on exact cover ( 3 / 9 3/9 hits), MIS ( 9 / 12 9/12 ), Wishart ( 5 / 9 5/9 ) and one dense-ER instance ( 11 / 12 11/12 ), while matching the classical result on the other families. The adaptive-depth check covers all 27 benchmark instances at actual n = 32 n=32 , yielding 3 / 12 3/12 hits on newly covered instances and 13 / 15 13/15 on previously covered instances (App. 11.2 ). Simulation wall-clock time measures classical computational cost. Quantum-circuit depth is a separate hardware-relevant resource estimate, not a complete measure of quantum runtime Dehn et al. (2026) . This is a negative result for the fixed-schedule protocol tested, not for all QAOA variants, since angle optimisation, warm starts and recursive methods are outside scope. A separate MPS simulation-convergence test uses six gauge-randomised Wishart instances at n = 40 , 48 n=40,48 . All tested bond caps saturate, sampled energies do not converge as the cap increases, and no run reaches the optimum. A deeper probe is available for only one instance. These runs therefore do not provide a converged LR-QAOA simulation on the dense larger instances (details are in App. 11.2 ).

sections.heading: 5.2 Small-size success-probability scaling (Campaign D)
sections.text: An LR-QAOA layer count proportional to size would give polynomial gate-level circuit depth on all-to-all connectivity, but an efficient solver also requires adequate success probability. We test that premise at small sizes. The conditional resource calculation and exploratory candidate indicator are given in App. 11.3 . We compute the exact probability mass on the full optimal manifold for n = 8 n=8 – 16 16 , across ten families and three seeds, at p = 12 , n , 2 ​ n p=12,n,2n . The 450 exact statevector measurements evaluate probability mass rather than the polished sampled energies used in Campaign A. The fitted slopes of log 2 ⁡ P opt \log_{2}P_{\mathrm{opt}} are − 0.32 , − 0.21 , − 0.15 -0.32,-0.21,-0.15 bits per qubit, respectively: increasing depth slows the decay, but at p = n p=n the probability still halves about every five qubits. Against the pre-registered criterion, which counted | σ | ≤ 0.1 |\sigma|\leq 0.1 as support and σ ≤ − 0.25 \sigma\leq-0.25 as refutation, this result is inconclusive, not a confirmation of constant success probability. The family breakdown is consequential: six families are near-flat, but the slopes at p = n p=n remain negative for exact cover ( − 0.75 -0.75 ), MIS ( − 0.54 -0.54 ) and Wishart ( − 0.29 -0.29 ), including the family proposed as the first quantum target. All three lie below the refutation threshold of − 0.25 -0.25 . The criterion was registered for the pooled slope, so this family-level reading is descriptive, but it points against the premise on Wishart rather than leaving it open. The quantum-candidate region and its polynomial-depth interpretation must therefore remain conditional: our small-size data do not support the required scaling premise on Wishart. The measurement window is narrow, however, so it cannot rule out asymptotic softening of the decay rate. Figure 6 shows the decline across the tested depth schedules. sections.heading: 6 Wishart hardness–size–budget scaling
sections.text: Campaign E extends the gauged Wishart comparison to larger sizes and a second hardness setting. The planted optimum supplies a reference independent of solver success, allowing search and certification to be tested directly rather than inferred from structural diagnostics.

sections.heading: 7 Discussion
sections.text: The campaigns distinguish search, certification, and diagnostic explanation. Campaign A establishes a strong branch-and-cut baseline: it matches every reference energy and certifies 176 of 180 benchmark instances. Campaign B qualifies that comparison. On the enlarged gauged Wishart set, PT reaches optima that branch-and-cut misses within its budget, although it cannot provide certificates. The preferred method therefore depends on the required outcome and the instance setting, not only on the variable count. The Campaign A diagnostics rank TN representation demand and provide a coarse runtime estimate, but do not yield a useful solver-selection rule. Campaign C identifies excited-state trapping and demonstrates reset mitigation on the evaluated cases. Among the 81 mitigation-clean out-of-sample instances, one fails at χ = 4 \chi=4 and none at χ = 16 \chi=16 . However, failures remain in the full 90-instance out-of-sample set, so the results on the 81 mitigation-clean instances do not establish that representation-capacity limits or optimisation failures have been eliminated in general. The 105 LR-QAOA simulation runs in Campaign A show no solution-quality improvement over the classical comparators. Campaign D extends coverage and tests simulation and probability-scaling assumptions, without establishing an efficient quantum solver on Wishart. Campaign E supplies a separate classical scaling comparison: at α = 0.5 \alpha=0.5 , none of the tested methods reaches the planted optimum at sampled sizes from n = 72 n=72 onward within the tested budgets. This identifies a setting for further comparison, rather than evidence of quantum advantage.

sections.heading: 7.1 Threats to validity
sections.text: The heuristic comparison depends on the solver portfolio and budget. In Campaign B’s enlarged gauged set at n = 48 n=48 , the reported hit rate rises from SA’s 0.25 0.25 to PT’s 0.44 0.44 at a 0.75 0.75 s allocation and to 1.00 1.00 at 60 60 s per PT run. In Campaign E, increasing the PT budget also extends search success on α = 0.7 \alpha=0.7 (Table 7 ). These comparisons concern the tested implementations and the budgets specified for each campaign, not heuristic optimisation in general. A portfolio solver, tabu search, or Burer–Monteiro relaxation could change the comparison further. The Wishart generator places its planted optimum at x = 0 x=0 , the trivial incumbent of the mixed-integer program. On those instances the exact solver starts at the answer and only the bound is work, which flatters it. SA is affected too, through its temperature schedule. Its start temperature T 0 = max ⁡ ∑ j i ⁡ | Q i ​ j | T_{0}=\max_{i}\sum_{j}|Q_{ij}| reads the diagonal of Q Q , which the gauge transformation changes, whereas its other steps (uniform random start, Metropolis acceptance on energy differences) are gauge-equivariant. In a control with ten independent runs on each of the ten instances per size, SA’s rate at n = 48 n=48 falls from 0.44 0.44 on the planted instances to 0.25 0.25 on the gauged ones (exact sign test over instances, p = 0.008 p=0.008 ). Running the gauged instances with the planted frame’s T 0 T_{0} restores it to 0.39 0.39 . At n = 40 n=40 the frames do not differ ( 0.63 0.63 in both). Part of SA’s gauged deficit at n = 48 n=48 therefore reflects its schedule rather than the landscape. Campaign A uses ungauged Wishart instances (Table 5 ). Campaign B distinguishes paired and enlarged gauged comparisons (Table 6 ), and Campaign E uses gauged instances throughout. The separate paired gauging control used three instances per size. At n = 48 n=48 , the exact solver’s reach in that small sample falls from 3 3 of 3 3 on planted instances to 1 1 of 3 3 after gauge transformation. SA’s Campaign A one-hit-in-six result is a single-run summary on the ungauged Wishart instances. Ten additional runs per instance give a pooled hit rate of 0.53 0.53 . TN repeatability was checked only on a restricted ungauged subset and does not establish general repeatability (Sec. 3.2 ). Likewise, SA’s 900/900 calibration hits do not justify assuming that single runs are representative on harder instances. The enlarged gauged comparison in Campaign B uses ten instances per size, while its TN recheck covers three. Campaign E has its own sample counts, including only one instance at n = 128 n=128 . The denominators and replication therefore differ across claims. For example, the LR-QAOA comparison’s exact-cover hit count is 3 / 9 3/9 . App. 9 summarises replication. These limited samples and the reporting issues noted with the protocols constrain generalisation beyond the tested instances. Wall-clock comparisons reflect implementation, threading, and system load as well as algorithmic work. Gurobi uses compiled solver code. SA and PT use Python update loops, while TN uses compiled numerical routines through Python. Shared language alone does not remove these differences. Timing boundaries also differ: the Campaign A exact baseline times optimisation, heuristic run times include the full solver call, and PT excludes replica initialisation. These differences limit the interpretation of cross-solver runtime ratios. Campaign A’s MPS simulation of LR-QAOA is limited by fixed depth and the gate-count guard. Campaign D improves coverage at n = 32 n=32 by changing depth. Its newly covered dense cases use p = 6 p=6 – 11 11 . The separate n = 40 , 48 n=40,48 probes do not establish convergence of the truncated MPS simulation of LR-QAOA (App. 11.2 ). These limitations concern the tested simulations and do not establish LR-QAOA performance on hardware. The success-probability scaling premise is also unconfirmed in the measured window (Sec. 5.2 ). Our LR-QAOA simulations do not model device noise, and the circuit-depth estimates do not by themselves establish performance on noisy hardware. Stilck França and García-Patrón Stilck França and García-Patrón (2021) derive limits on noisy quantum optimisation that depend on the noise level and the relation between problem and device connectivity. Their results motivate treating noise and connectivity explicitly in a hardware comparison. We do not evaluate those bounds for the instances studied here. The Campaign A calibration and evaluation sets differ structurally because the split by size was intentional for the extrapolation question, but it means the two sets are not exchangeable. SA reaches the optimum in every calibration run, in 96 % 96\% of out-of-sample runs, and on Wishart out-of-sample in 66 % 66\% . A quality model fitted where nothing fails cannot learn what failure looks like, which is exactly the obstruction App. 12 runs into. Campaign A covers ten synthetic families up to n = 48 n=48 . Its solver comparison need not transfer to industrial instances or other size ranges. Campaign E extends the evidence to larger Wishart instances, but its failures remain statements about tested budgets, not proofs of intractability. The default exact-solver cap is ten minutes, with one-hour limits on selected instances as specified in Sec. 6 . Fixed-budget comparisons alone do not establish asymptotic advantage Rønnow et al. (2014) . The conditional quantum-resource projection in App. 11.3 also depends on family-specific success-probability scaling. The cited LR-QAOA study reports favourable behaviour for fully-connected weighted Max-Cut, but not its Max-2-SAT family Montañez-Barrera and Michielsen (2025) . Campaign D does not establish the required premise for Wishart in the measured small-size window. Campaign E supplies classical evidence only. A direct quantum test on the larger gauged Wishart instances remains necessary. Finally, the evaluated success-probability weighting does not improve the Campaign A cost ranking (Sec. 4.3 ). Campaign B shows why isolated SA runs cannot support stable solver recommendations, and why PT belongs in the comparison.

sections.heading: 8 Conclusions
sections.text: The comparison of QUBO solvers depends on whether the objective is to find a solution or to certify its optimality. In Campaign A, with 180 benchmark instances, general-purpose branch-and-cut matches every reference energy and proves optimality on 176 instances within the 600 600 s cap, including 86 larger instances outside the enumeration range used here. This establishes a strong exact-solver baseline for the tested families and sizes, rather than a universal recommendation based on variable count. The gauge-randomised Wishart controls in Campaign B show why the distinction between search and certification is essential. At n = 40 n=40 , branch-and-cut certifies seven of ten optima. At n = 48 n=48 , it finds four of ten and certifies none within its budget. PT, given 60 60 s per run, reaches every optimum in every tested run on this enlarged control set, but provides no certificate. Thus the method that supplies proofs need not be the most effective method for finding solutions within a given budget. The Campaign A trajectory diagnostics provide a cost estimate, and Campaign C provides an explanation of a solver failure. A treewidth bound ranks the tensor-network trajectory’s bond-dimension demand, although a tighter runtime estimate requires the measured bond dimension. Controlled experiments show that warm-started DMRG can follow an excited branch and that resets resolve the failures in the targeted mitigation study. Failures remain in the broader out-of-sample evaluation, however, so the reset procedure does not eliminate trapping in general. Entanglement and magic provide distinct, moderately correlated descriptions of the measured trajectories. These results support diagnostic use of the features, but the evaluated cost models do not improve solver selection over the always-SA baseline. The tested LR-QAOA runs show no solution-quality advantage over the classical comparators. Campaign E extends the classical comparison to n = 128 n=128 : on the harder setting ( α = 0.5 \alpha=0.5 ), none of the tested classical methods reaches the planted optimum at the sampled sizes from n = 72 n=72 onward. This is a result for the tested implementations and budgets, with one-hour exact-solver runs on selected sizes, not a bound on classical optimisation in general. It identifies a concrete regime for further comparison without establishing a quantum advantage. In particular, the small-size measurements in Campaign D do not establish the success-probability scaling needed to make LR-QAOA efficient on Wishart instances. A direct quantum evaluation in this regime, together with stronger classical baselines and estimates of success probability at comparable computational budgets, is needed to determine whether an advantage exists.

sections.heading: 9 Reproducibility
sections.text: All wall-clock figures quoted in this paper were measured on one machine: an Intel Core Ultra 9 285H (16 logical cores) with 15 15 GB of RAM available to a WSL2 Linux guest (kernel 6.6.87), running Python 3.12.12 with NumPy 2.3.5, SciPy 1.16.3, quimb 1.11.2 and networkx 3.6.1. The exact solver is Gurobi 13.0.2. The code base records this environment in machine-readable form. Implementation differences across the solvers are discussed in Sec. 2.4 . Main-benchmark budgets and replication are given in Table 2 . Campaign B protocols are specified in Secs. 3.2 and 3.3 . Campaign D protocols are given in Sec. 5.2 and App. 11.2 . Campaign E contains 61 distinct instances and 610 distinct SA instance/seed combinations. Its stored SA and PT repeat files also contain six replayed batches with identical seeds; all reported rates count only the first batch per instance (Sec. 6 ). The treatment of PT results carried forward from shorter budgets is specified in the same section.

sections.heading: 10 Solver configuration details
sections.text: This appendix gives the numerical settings and implementation checks for the solvers introduced in Sec. 2.4 .

sections.heading: Exact solver.
sections.text: We minimise x T ​ Q ​ x x^{T}Qx over binary variables using Gurobi Kochenberger et al. (2014) ; Gurobi Optimization, LLC (2024) , with either the standard product linearisation or the native binary-quadratic objective. The saved main baseline uses 165 linearised and 15 native quadratic models. The latter are the SK and Wishart instances at n = 40 , 48 n=40,48 and the random-frustrated instances at n = 48 n=48 , whose earlier linearised attempts encountered the solver’s licence-size limit. The linearised objective is checked against exhaustive enumeration at small sizes. For each instance, we use the result from the final successful solver invocation. At termination, the baseline records the best feasible solution, remaining MIP gap, solver status, and elapsed optimisation time. Reaching the reference energy and certifying optimality are separate outcomes. The certificate flag means that Gurobi returned OPTIMAL under its numerical tolerances, with the default relative MIP-gap tolerance of 10 − 4 10^{-4} . Four of the 176 flagged records have nonzero relative MIP gaps, ranging from 8.66 × 10 − 7 8.66\times 10^{-7} to 9.06 × 10 − 5 9.06\times 10^{-5} ; all lie below this tolerance, and we count them as certified. As an upper limit, these runs are capped at 600 600 s.

sections.heading: Simulated annealing.
sections.text: SA Kirkpatrick et al. (1983) uses single-flip Metropolis updates with R = 4 R=4 restarts and n sw = 2000 n_{\mathrm{sw}}=2000 sweeps per restart. A sweep proposes one flip at each of the n n sites in random order, giving 8000 ​ n 8000n proposed updates per run. The geometric temperature schedule starts at T 0 = max ⁡ ∑ j i ⁡ | Q i ​ j | + 10 − 12 T_{0}=\max_{i}\sum_{j}|Q_{ij}|+10^{-12} and ends at T 1 = 10 − 3 T_{1}=10^{-3} , with ratio ( T 1 / T 0 ) 1 / ( n sw − 1 ) (T_{1}/T_{0})^{1/(n_{\mathrm{sw}}-1)} . Because T 0 T_{0} includes the diagonal of Q Q , it is not invariant under the gauge transformation; Sec. 7.1 quantifies the effect. The best state from each restart is refined by first-improvement descent, and the best result is returned. Reference-energy generation also uses R = 8 R=8 and n sw = 4000 n_{\mathrm{sw}}=4000 , giving four times as many proposed updates.

sections.heading: Parallel tempering.
sections.text: PT uses 16 replicas on a geometric temperature ladder. Its hot endpoint is T max = max ⁡ ∑ j i ⁡ | Q i ​ j | + 10 − 12 T_{\max}=\max_{i}\sum_{j}|Q_{ij}|+10^{-12} . Its cold endpoint is T min = max ⁡ ( min i ≠ j , Q i ​ j ≠ 0 ⁡ | Q i ​ j | / 10 , 10 − 6 ) T_{\min}=\max(\min_{i\neq j,Q_{ij}\neq 0}|Q_{ij}|/10,10^{-6}) . For a matrix without off-diagonal couplings, T max / 100 T_{\max}/100 replaces the inner minimum before applying the floor. Each replica performs random-order single-flip Metropolis updates. After every sweep, all neighbouring replica pairs attempt exchanges sequentially. No final local-search polish is applied. Repetition seeds are 1000 ​ ( k + 1 ) 1000(k+1) . The clock starts after replica initialisation and is checked after each complete sweep and exchange pass, permitting a small overshoot. A time budget supersedes the ordinary sweep limit. Main-benchmark runs use a fixed 0.75 0.75 s allocation rather than matching each instance’s measured SA time. Control budgets and repetitions are specified in Sec. 3.3 . On the gauged Wishart instances at n = 40 n=40 and 48 48 , with 0.75 0.75 s per run, the median swap acceptance was 0.08 0.08 with eight replicas and 0.27 0.27 with 16; with eight, too few exchanges are accepted for the ladder to work, so all reported PT runs use 16. Acceptance in other runs varies with instance and budget. The stored PT records do not include the replica count. For the Campaign A and B results it is fixed by the labelled result files; for Campaign E it rests on the documented run command ( --replicas 16 ).

sections.heading: Tensor-network anneal.
sections.text: The TN solver uses two-site DMRG on a matrix-product-operator representation of H ⁡ ( s ) H(s) White (1992) ; Schollwöck (2011) , checked against an independent dense construction at n = 6 n=6 . It uses an 11-point interpolation grid, with more points near s = 1 s=1 , and warm-starts each point from the preceding MPS. A cold-start reset may replace that state when it finds a lower energy. The mitigation study is described in Sec. 4.2 . The primary TN solver uses χ = 32 \chi=32 on all 180 benchmark instances. Its energies and wall-clock times supply the main comparison and runtime-model fits. Separate runs at χ = 4 , 8 , 16 \chi=4,8,16 provide the capacity study. All four solver configurations enable reset checks, using the common grid s ∈ { 0 , 0.16 , 0.32 , 0.48 , 0.64 , 0.80 , 0.84 , 0.88 , 0.92 , 0.96 , 1 } . s\in\{0,0.16,0.32,0.48,0.64,0.80,0.84,0.88,0.92,0.96,1\}. DMRG uses truncation cutoff 10 − 10 10^{-10} , convergence tolerance 10 − 8 10^{-8} , and at most 30 sweeps per point. At every grid point with s ≥ 0.5 s\geq 0.5 , a cold probe with χ ≤ 16 \chi\leq 16 and at most ten sweeps tests for an energy improvement exceeding 10 − 6 ​ max ⁡ ( 1 , | E | ) 10^{-6}\max(1,|E|) . If successful, the state is refined at the solver’s full bond cap and accepted only if it retains that improvement. Sites follow the input variable order. A degenerate optimum may be represented by a superposition, so single-site expectation values need not identify an optimal bitstring. The readout therefore considers eight direct MPS samples, the sign vector of ⟨ Z i ⟩ \langle Z_{i}\rangle and its global flip, and four random resolutions of sites with near-zero expectation values. Each candidate is refined by single-flip local search and the lowest energy is returned. The near-zero condition is | m i | < 0.25 ​ ( max j ⁡ | m j | + 10 − 12 ) |m_{i}|<0.25(\max_{j}|m_{j}|+10^{-12}) , where m i m_{i} is the magnetisation returned by the MPS library. Sampling, random resolutions, and polishing use the instance seed in the primary single-anneal run.

sections.text: LR-QAOA uses the fixed linear schedules γ k = ( k / p ) ​ Δ \gamma_{k}=(k/p)\Delta and β k = ( 1 − k / p ) ​ Δ \beta_{k}=(1-k/p)\Delta , k = 1 , … , p k=1,\ldots,p , on the coefficient-normalised Hamiltonian Montañez-Barrera and Michielsen (2025) . Here p p is the layer count and Δ \Delta is the schedule amplitude. The nonconstant Ising coefficients are divided by max ⁡ ( max i < j ⁡ | J i ​ j | , max i ⁡ | h i | , 10 − 12 ) \max(\max_{i<j}|J_{ij}|,\max_{i}|h_{i}|,10^{-12}) . Each layer applies the cost unitary followed by the mixer exp ( + i β k ∑ i X i ) \exp(+i\beta_{k}\sum_{i}X_{i}) , starting from | + ⟩ ⊗ n \lvert+\rangle^{\otimes n} . The Campaign A configurations and eligibility limits are given in Table 2 . Integer division of the nominal 4000-shot budget gives 666 samples per setting, or 3996 in total. The MPS runs use a truncation cutoff of 10 − 10 10^{-10} . The 3000-gate guard counts logical two-qubit cost gates ( p ​ m pm here), excluding single-qubit gates and routing overhead. The observed data records 75 instances as SA fallbacks. Their exclusion is described in Sec. 2.4 . Supplementary Campaign D protocols are specified in App. 11.2 and Sec. 5.2 . The MPS implementation of LR-QAOA reproduces the statevector implementation at n = 10 n=10 with ample bond dimension, checking gate conventions and the mixer sign. Larger-instance convergence is assessed separately in App. 11.2 .

sections.heading: 11.1 Spectral protocols and capacity-failure breakdown
sections.text: The spectral routines use sparse Lanczos diagonalisation with at most 5000 iterations and no explicit override of the eigensolver tolerance. The gap-versus-failure study uses 15 points from s = 0.3 s=0.3 to 0.97 0.97 on 3-regular instances at n = 14 , 18 n=14,18 , with seeds 0 , 1 , 2 0,1,2 , and six anneals per instance. It tested whether a small minimum Δ g \Delta_{g} predicts trapping. The pre-registered verdict was negative. With four instances showing trapping and two without, the sample is below the AUC reporting threshold of Sec. 2.5.4 , so we give the pattern instead. At an essentially fixed minimum Δ g ≈ 0.28 \Delta_{g}\approx 0.28 – 0.30 0.30 , the trap rate rose from at most 1 / 3 1/3 at n = 14 n=14 to at least 5 / 6 5/6 at n = 18 n=18 . Two of the six instances have endpoint degeneracy g = 12 g=12 and 18 18 ; for them Δ g \Delta_{g} measures the distance to the 13th or 19th level, not an excitation gap at intermediate s s , so their values ( 0.63 0.63 , 0.69 0.69 ) are not comparable with the g = 2 g=2 cases. The negative verdict is therefore weak evidence; the trapping account in Sec. 4.2 rests on the trajectory comparison of Fig. 5 , not on gap magnitudes. The trapping figure instead evaluates four low-lying levels on its 17-point solver grid, using exact diagonal energies at s = 1 s=1 . Comparing χ = 4 \chi=4 and 16 16 across all 90 90 out-of-sample instances, six failures at both caps are flagged as trapped, one more is cured at χ = 16 \chi=16 , and one fails only at that larger cap. This non-nested pattern points to residual trapping rather than a simple capacity limit. Accordingly, χ 99 max \chi_{99}^{\max} does not meet the pre-registered AUC target of 0.9 0.9 as a capacity-failure predictor (with capacity failure as the positive class and larger χ 99 max \chi_{99}^{\max} as the higher-risk score, AUC 0.88 0.88 in sample and 0.74 0.74 out of sample): capacity failures are too rare for reliable discrimination.

sections.heading: 11.2 Supplementary LR-QAOA coverage and convergence checks
sections.text: The adaptive-depth experiment retains χ = 32 \chi=32 , Δ = 0.5 \Delta=0.5 , and 500 samples, with p = min ⁡ ( 64 , ⌊ 3000 / m ⌋ ) p=\min(64,\lfloor 3000/m\rfloor) . It covers all 27 main-benchmark instances with actual n = 32 n=32 . The corresponding grid instances have n = 35 n=35 and are excluded. These runs supplement, rather than replace, the Campaign A fixed-depth comparison. The convergence probes use six gauge-randomised Wishart instances at n = 40 , 48 n=40,48 , with gauge seeds different from those of Campaign B. Eighteen usable runs compare χ = 8 , 16 , 32 \chi=8,16,32 at p = 8 p=8 . One additional usable run uses p = 40 p=40 , χ = 32 \chi=32 at n = 40 n=40 . Two additional attempts terminate with singular-value-decomposition (SVD) errors and provide no convergence evidence. The coverage and convergence outcomes are reported in Sec. 5.1 .

sections.heading: 11.3 Exploratory candidate indicator and conditional resource projection
sections.text: These analyses use main-benchmark diagnostics and a conditional quantum-circuit resource calculation. They are not additional solver campaigns or validated rules for predicting quantum advantage. We use the structural indicator 𝒬 ⁡ ( Q ) = [ ρ G ≥ 0.9 ] ⏟ TN priced out ∧ [ D J ≥ 5 ] ∧ [ h LM ≤ 0.3 ] ⏟ wide-range, rugged ∧ [ M 2 max ≥ 8 bits ] ⏟ no Clifford shortcut , \mathcal{Q}(Q)=\underbrace{[\rho_{G}\geq 0.9]}_{\text{TN priced out}}\wedge\underbrace{[D_{J}\geq 5]\wedge[h_{\mathrm{LM}}\leq 0.3]}_{\text{wide-range, rugged}}\wedge\underbrace{[M_{2}^{\max}\geq 8\ \text{bits}]}_{\text{no Clifford shortcut}}, (8) to mark candidate instances where the measured classical routes are strained. Its components combine dense-graph/treewidth structure, a wide coupling range with a rugged local-minimum landscape (a static profile shared by the Wishart, SK and random-frustrated ensembles, not a measured predictor of SA failure), and a magic barrier that excludes stabilizer-based simulation. All four thresholds were chosen on the Campaign A data, against the six SA misses that the indicator is then scored on. Its perfect recall is therefore an in-sample property, not a validated detection rate. Precision is 0.33 0.33 (Fig. 8 ): nine false positives are SK instances and three are Wishart instances on which SA succeeds. These structural twins show why 𝒬 \mathcal{Q} marks a candidate region rather than predicting failure per instance. It is a separate diagnostic, not a runtime-based solver recommendation. Figure 8: The quantum-candidate indicator in the D J D_{J} – M 2 max M_{2}^{\max} plane. The selected region (orange circles) captures every Campaign A instance where SA fails against the reference optimum (red stars, all Wishart at n ≥ 32 n\geq 32 ) at in-sample recall 1.0 1.0 , but also twelve instances on which SA succeeds ( 9 9 Sherrington–Kirkpatrick structural twins and 3 3 Wishart), indistinguishable by static features (precision 0.33 0.33 ). Grey dots are the remaining instances of the Campaign A benchmark: not selected by the indicator, and solved by simulated annealing. The asymptotic argument is conditional. On all-to-all connectivity, the R Z ​ Z R_{ZZ} gates can be scheduled in χ edge ​ ( G ) \chi_{\mathrm{edge}}(G) rounds, the edge-chromatic number of G G . By Vizing’s theorem Vizing (1964) , this is at most d max ​ ( G ) + 1 d_{\max}(G)+1 , where d max ​ ( G ) d_{\max}(G) is the maximum vertex degree. Including one mixer round per LR-QAOA layer, the gate-level circuit depth is D = 1 + p ⁡ [ χ edge ​ ( G ) + 1 ] ≤ 1 + p ⁡ [ d max ​ ( G ) + 2 ] , D=1+p\,[\chi_{\mathrm{edge}}(G)+1]\leq 1+p\,[d_{\max}(G)+2], (9) with p ​ m pm two-qubit gates. The literature reports near-constant success probability at p ∼ n p\sim n for several families Montañez-Barrera and Michielsen (2025) . If this carries over to Wishart, dense-instance depth grows as D ∼ n 2 D\sim n^{2} . The relevant classical comparison would then be exact contraction, whose cost grows as exp ⁡ [ O ⁡ ( tw ) ] \exp[O(\mathrm{tw})] with tw ∼ n \mathrm{tw}\sim n on dense graphs, not the bond-capped DMRG anneal of this paper, whose cost is polynomial in n n at fixed χ \chi and which carries no optimality guarantee. That premise is not established here.

sections.heading: 12 Cost models and limits of heuristic selection
sections.text: This appendix documents the selection procedure evaluated in Sec. 4.3 , as implemented in the accompanying code. It has two stages. The first asks whether cheap Tier-0 features already guarantee that an exact method is affordable. If so, there is nothing to select: the instance is solved exactly, with a proof, and no heuristic is considered. Only instances that this exactness check leaves unsettled reach the second stage, which ranks the heuristics by predicted runtime. The distinction matters for reading the results: the retrospective cost analysis below also covers instances that the first stage would settle, so it evaluates more instances than the procedure would actually rank. The deployed exactness check applies four sufficient conditions in order (Table 8 ). If one applies, it returns an exact method and no heuristic cost is estimated. The cost fits below are a retrospective analysis of observed timings on the calibration set, including instances that the deployed n ≤ 30 n\leq 30 rule would settle before cost ranking. In deployment, these cost laws apply only after the exactness check leaves an instance unsettled. The tensor-network law scatters, and scatters much further when the bond dimension is inferred from the treewidth bound (Tier-0 only) instead of measured. Its largest out-of-sample predictions then exceed the measured times by three orders of magnitude. Brute force appears on the calibration split only: the enumerator is not run at n ≥ 32 n\geq 32 . The cost ranking P ∗ ​ ( Q ) = arg ⁡ min P ​ t ^ P ​ ( Q ) P^{*}(Q)=\arg\min_{P}\hat{t}_{P}(Q) is evaluated against the ex-post heuristic labels in Sec. 4.3 . Under the fitted nominal budgets, the TN-to-SA predicted runtime ratio is approximately 1.008 ​ χ ^ 3 1.008\hat{\chi}^{3} , so this benchmark’s ranking favours SA regardless of instance. This reflects the compared budgets and fitted constants, not a general result about the paradigms. Weighting runtime by a predicted hit probability also failed to improve the ranking. The calibration set has no failures, so a model fitted there predicts unit hit probability and leaves the ranking unchanged. An exploratory fit using all instances likewise left the 85/90 score unchanged. A hard probability cutoff reduced it. Together with the Wishart–SK feature twins, this indicates that static features in this benchmark do not supply the quality signal needed to repair the Campaign A ranking.
