We compare classical, tensor-network, and fixed-schedule quantum approaches on 180 benchmark instances from ten families with 14–48 variables, supplemented by harder synthetic instances with known optimal solutions, extending to 128 variables. On the main benchmark, a general-purpose branch-and-cut solver matches all reference energies and certifies 176 instances within a 600 s cap. When the known optima are moved to randomly chosen bitstrings, the search comparison changes: at n = 48 n=48 the branch-and-cut solver finds only four of ten optima and certifies none, whereas parallel tempering reaches every optimum in every tested run at a 60 s budget. Structural and trajectory diagnostics explain aspects of tensor-network performance. A treewidth bound ranks trajectory bond-dimension demand at Spearman ρ = 0.78 \rho=0.78 in sample and 0.73 0.73 out of sample, but provides only a coarse runtime estimate. Controlled experiments identify excited-state trapping during warm-started density-matrix renormalization group (DMRG) sweeps and demonstrate mitigation by restarting the variational search. These diagnostics do not yield a validated solver-selection rule. The tested linear-ramp quantum approximate optimization algorithm (LR-QAOA) runs offer no solution-quality improvement over the classical comparators. In the separate Wishart scaling study, on the harder setting, none of the classical methods tested reaches the optimum at the sampled sizes from n = 72 n=72 onward within the tested budgets. While this does not provide evidence for quantum advantage, it identifies a domain for further investigation. keywords QUBO, combinatorial optimisation, algorithm selection, tensor networks, QAOA, benchmarking 1 Introduction Quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) provides a common formulation for comparing classical, tensor-network, and quantum approaches to combinatorial optimisation Kochenberger et al. (2014) ; Lucas (2014) . For a practitioner, choosing a method requires specifying the desired outcome: a low-energy solution, an optimum, or a certificate that no better solution exists. These objectives need not favour the same solver. A meaningful comparison must therefore distinguish solution quality from optimality certification and relate both to the computational budget. These considerations connect to algorithm selection Bischl et al. (2016) , which has been investigated for classical QUBO portfolios Dunning et al. (2018) . Here, we focus on comparing solution quality, optimality certification, and computational cost across solver approaches, and on understanding how instance structure and trajectory diagnostics relate to their performance. Problem instance structure offers a possible basis for making this choice. Properties of the interaction graph can constrain the cost of exact methods and may indicate the resources required by tensor-network algorithms Markov and Shi (2008) ; Schollwöck (2011) . Quantum-information diagnostics offer a complementary perspective, but their interpretation requires care. Alongside entanglement, we measure non-stabilizerness, often called magic : a quantum resource that characterises departures from stabilizer states, which admit efficient classical simulation Gottesman (1998) ; Aaronson and Gottesman (2004) ; Leone et al. (2022) . Magic concerns the resources needed for stabilizer-based simulation but high magic alone (e.g., with low entanglement) does not rule out efficient classical simulation by methods that do not rely on a stabilizer representation. Every QUBO optimum can be represented by a computational-basis state with neither entanglement nor magic. The relevant resources consequently arise in the intermediate states explored by an algorithm, rather than in the optimal bitstring itself Dupont et al. (2022b) ; Dupont et al. (2022a) ; Capecci et al. (2025) . We study these resources along a transverse-field interpolation connecting a simple initial Hamiltonian to the QUBO Hamiltonian Kadowaki and Nishimori (1998) ; Albash and Lidar (2018) . This paper investigates how much structural and trajectory information can explain solver performance, and whether it supports useful choices between methods. We compare a general-purpose branch-and-cut solver (Gurobi) Gurobi Optimization, LLC (2024) , simulated annealing (SA) Kirkpatrick et al. (1983) , a density-matrix renormalization group (DMRG) based tensor-network (TN) anneal White (1992) ; Schollwöck (2011) , and fixed-schedule linear-ramp quantum approximate optimization (LR-QAOA) Farhi et al. (2014) ; Montañez-Barrera and Michielsen (2025) , with parallel tempering (PT) Swendsen and Wang (1986) ; Hukushima and Nemoto (1996) providing an additional classical comparison. Each serves a specific role: branch-and-cut supplies a baseline capable of certification, SA supplies a simple thermal-search baseline and PT tests whether SA’s failures persist under a stronger thermal method. The DMRG anneal probes variational optimisation of matrix-product states (MPS), while LR-QAOA probes a quantum-circuit approach with prescribed parameters. The shared Hamiltonian interpolation connects these last two methods, although their computational procedures and intermediate states remain distinct. Our main benchmark (Campaign A) comprises 180 instances from ten problem families with n = 14 n=14 – 48 48 variables. It includes 90 small calibration instances with exhaustively verified optima and 90 larger instances used to assess extrapolation; the latter also receive an exact-solver cross-check (Sec. 2.3 ). The robustness controls (Campaign B) and scaling study (Campaign E) also use the Wishart-planted family Hamze et al. (2020) : synthetic problems constructed from random Gaussian vectors so that a chosen solution is guaranteed to be optimal, with a parameter controlling problem difficulty. These known optima provide reference targets beyond the range of exhaustive enumeration. To avoid giving solvers an easily guessed target, we randomly complement selected binary variables ( x i ↦ 1 − x i x_{i}\mapsto 1-x_{i} ) and transform the objective accordingly. This relabelling, called gauge randomisation , moves the planted optimum from the all-zero bitstring to a random bitstring while preserving the energy landscape. It controls for the advantage a solver may gain from the original placement of the solution Mandrà and Katzgraber (2018) . These experiments examine the robustness of the comparison and extend the study to n = 128 n=128 (Secs. 3.3 and 6 ). The results distinguish three aspects of solver performance. First, branch-and-cut provides a strong baseline in Campaign A, matching every reference energy and certifying nearly all instances. Its advantage nevertheless depends on whether the task is search or certification: on the harder gauge-randomised instances, PT can find optima that branch-and-cut misses within its allotted budget (Secs. 3.3 and 6 ). Second, a cheap treewidth bound of the QUBO interaction graph ranks the bond-dimension demand of the tensor-network trajectories, but supplies only a coarse runtime estimate. The evaluated structural features and cost models do not produce a useful solver-selection rule (Sec. 4.3 ). Controlled experiments further identify excited-state trapping during warm-started DMRG sweeps as a failure mechanism that can be mitigated by restarting the variational search (Sec. 4 ). Entanglement and magic are only moderately correlated in the measured trajectories and provide distinct diagnostic information. Third, the tested LR-QAOA runs provide no solution-quality improvement over the classical comparators (Sec. 5 ). The larger Wishart experiments identify instances on which the tested classical methods struggle, offering a concrete setting for further quantum–classical comparisons. Together, these findings establish a classical baseline, clarify what trajectory diagnostics can explain, and identify the additional evidence needed for meaningful solver selection across computational approaches. Section 2 defines the shared framework and summarises Campaigns A–E. Section 3 presents the main benchmark and robustness controls (A and B). Section 4 brings together the benchmark diagnostics and targeted TN mechanism tests (C). Section 5 reports the LR-QAOA comparison and supplementary quantum studies (D), followed by the Wishart scaling study (E) in Sec. 6 . Supporting experiments and exploratory resource projections are collected in App. 11 . 2 Problem formulation and experimental framework This section defines the optimisation problem, the benchmark instances, and the common evaluation framework. We distinguish solution quality, optimality certification, and computational cost. The main benchmark provides the basis for the solver comparison and predictive analyses; additional campaigns examine robustness, tensor-network failure mechanisms, LR-QAOA protocols, and scaling to harder instances. Section 2.6 summarises their questions and coverage. 2.1 QUBO formulation and Hamiltonian interpolation We consider QUBO instances defined by a real symmetric matrix Q ∈ ℝ n × n Q\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n} , with the objective E ∗ = min x ∈ { 0 , 1 } n ⁡ x T ​ Q ​ x . This interpolation provides a common Hamiltonian framework for the methods considered here. Quantum annealing evolves under a time-dependent Hamiltonian along this path. LR-QAOA uses alternating mixer and cost unitaries related to a discretisation of that evolution, with the coefficient normalisation and schedule specified in App. 10 . The DMRG anneal instead performs successive variational optimisations at selected values of s s . These procedures need not produce the same intermediate states. In particular, the entanglement measured along a DMRG sweep does not by itself bound the entanglement of the corresponding LR-QAOA circuit. The interpolation thus connects the computational approaches without identifying their intermediate states. To test sensitivity to this special placement, we use gauge-transformed variants: selected binary variables are complemented and the objective and reference energy are transformed accordingly. This moves the planted optimum to a generic bitstring while preserving the landscape up to relabelling and an accounted-for additive energy shift. The control subsets and repetitions are specified in Sec. 3.3 ; the larger scaling study has its own instance set and budgets. 2.3 Reference energies and optimality status We denote E ∗ = min x ∈ { 0 , 1 } n ⁡ x T ​ Q ​ x E^{*}=\min_{x\in\{0,1\}^{n}}x^{T}Qx as the true global minimum and additionally denote the benchmark target by E ref E_{\mathrm{ref}} . This reference energy is the objective value against which a solver’s returned solution is scored. When it is established by exhaustive enumeration, solver certification, an analytic argument, or a planted construction, E ref = E ∗ E_{\mathrm{ref}}=E^{*} . Otherwise it is the best-known feasible value, so E ref ≥ E ∗ E_{\mathrm{ref}}\geq E^{*} . A hit of a solver means matching E ref E_{\mathrm{ref}} within the tolerance defined in Sec. 2.5.4 ; it implies reaching the optimum only when the reference is known to be optimal. Solver-certified references use the numerical optimality convention specified in Sec. 2.4 . The reference construction and its optimality status depend on size and family. For all instance families at n ≤ 24 n\leq 24 , exhaustive enumeration returns the exact optimum with a proof. All 90 calibration instances are of this kind. For Wishart, grid, exact cover, and ferro-chain instances at all sizes, the optimum is planted or known analytically, independently of any solver: the Wishart ensemble is generated around a chosen ground-state configuration Hamze et al. (2020) ; a bipartite grid Max-Cut has E ∗ = − m E^{*}=-m , where m m is the number of edges (every edge can be cut); the exact-cover instances are built around a hidden exact partition; and the ferromagnetic chain is minimised by the aligned configuration. These constructions provide E ref = E ∗ E_{\mathrm{ref}}=E^{*} for 36 of the 90 out-of-sample instances, without requiring exhaustive enumeration. The sole exception is one SK instance at n = 48 n=48 . In the additional Wishart experiments, including the larger scaling study, the references remain known optima by construction, independently of solver success. 2.4 Solver approaches and main-benchmark configurations We compare an exact optimisation baseline with thermal-search and tensor-network heuristics, and a quantum-circuit heuristic. Table 2 summarises their computational budgets. The descriptions below explain the choices needed to interpret the comparison; numerical settings and implementation checks are collected in App. 10 . Exact solver. Branch-and-cut searches restricted subproblems and uses bounds, strengthened by additional constraints, to discard regions that cannot improve the best solution found and ultimately certify optimality. We use Gurobi Kochenberger et al. (2014) ; Gurobi Optimization, LLC (2024) , which minimises the binary quadratic objective, using either a linearised or a native quadratic formulation, with a 600 600 s time limit. Finding the reference energy and certifying optimality are distinct outcomes: the reported certificate flag denotes the solver’s optimal status under its numerical tolerances (Sec. 2.3 ). Exhaustive enumeration provides an independent cross-check at small sizes. This general-purpose baseline does not establish the limits of exact optimisation: specialised branch-and-cut Rehfeldt et al. (2023) or methods exploiting low treewidth may perform better. Simulated annealing. SA Kirkpatrick et al. (1983) explores bitstrings through single-variable flips, accepting some energy increases to escape local minima. Metropolis acceptance becomes less permissive as the temperature falls. We use a geometric cooling schedule. Each run comprises four restarts of 2000 sweeps, where a sweep proposes one update per variable. The best state from each restart is refined by single-flip local search, and the lowest energy is returned. The extended runs used to establish reference energies receive four times this update budget. Parallel tempering. Similar to SA, PT Swendsen and Wang (1986) ; Hukushima and Nemoto (1996) runs several searches at different temperatures and exchanges configurations between them, allowing low-temperature searches to benefit from exploration at higher temperatures. As a second thermal-search baseline, we use 16 replicas with exchange attempts after every sweep. It uses a wall-clock budget and receives no final local-search polish. It is reported alongside SA but is not included in the retrospective heuristic winner labels or assigned a fitted runtime model. The main and control budgets are summarised in Table 2 and Sec. 3.3 . Tensor-network anneal. The TN anneal approximately minimises the interpolating Hamiltonian within a compact MPS representation, using each state as the starting point for the next interpolation step. We use two-site DMRG White (1992) ; Schollwöck (2011) , with bond dimension capped at χ = 32 \chi=32 . The bond dimension controls the size of the MPS representation and limits the entanglement it can represent. Cold-start checks mitigate excited-state trapping (Sec. 4 ). Several candidate bitstrings are extracted from the final MPS, each is refined by single-flip local search, and the lowest energy is returned. Separate runs at χ = 4 , 8 , 16 \chi=4,8,16 assess sensitivity to the bond cap. These optimisation runs all enable reset checks. The trajectory diagnostics use separate, reset-free sweeps (Sec. 2.5.2 ). LR-QAOA. LR-QAOA prepares a quantum state by alternating operations determined by the objective with operations that mix computational-basis states, then samples bitstrings as candidate solutions. It uses fixed linear parameter schedules on a coefficient-normalised Hamiltonian Montañez-Barrera and Michielsen (2025) . Here, a quantum circuit is the sequence of quantum gates that prepares the state before sampling. All LR-QAOA results reported in this paper are obtained by classical simulation of such circuits, none are quantum-hardware executions. The number of LR-QAOA layers is denoted by p p , and Δ \Delta sets the amplitude of the linear parameter schedules. With m m nonzero pairwise couplings, the LR-QAOA circuit uses p ​ m pm logical two-qubit cost gates. The layer count p p differs from the gate-level circuit depth D D , which also accounts for how gates within a layer are scheduled (App. 11.3 ). Campaign A uses exact statevector simulation for n ≤ 16 n\leq 16 and approximate MPS simulation for 16 < n ≤ 32 16<n\leq 32 , subject to a limit of 3000 logical two-qubit cost gates. Table 2 gives the depths and sampling budgets. Runs replaced by SA because of these limits are excluded from quantum comparisons. The lowest-energy sampled bitstring is selected and then polished once by single-flip local search. Unlike TN, this does not polish every candidate. The separate depth-scaling and adaptive-depth studies are discussed in Sec. 5 . Agreement between the statevector and MPS simulators at small size checks implementation conventions, but does not establish convergence of the larger MPS simulations. Nor do the DMRG trajectory diagnostics bound entanglement in the LR-QAOA states (Sec. 2.1 ). The MPS results must therefore be interpreted as approximate simulations of LR-QAOA.
